title: Document preview and file addresses
summary: Document preview separates watching a file (a shared resource observed by address) from reading its content (ordinary bounded host reads); the host resolves every path through the session filesystem.
firstReason: The host half (bounded, authorized reads) is kept; the observation half moves from a client resource hook to server-sent updates for the preview panel.

title: Client Session references, reference sources, and UI status
summary: In the browser, each view or operation holds its own counted reference to a client session object and names itself as the source; there is no global current session.
firstReason: The rule that there is no global current session is kept, but client-side session objects and reference counts are not needed when each rendered view is bound to a session id on the server.

title: Stable Sidebar tab mounting and Session retention
summary: A sidebar page that holds a live embedded browser keeps the same DOM ancestors through session switches, tab selection, pane moves, floating and docking, because Electron's webview resets its guest when it is disconnected from the document.
firstReason: The goal stands: an embedded page must not reload when the user switches tab or session. The mechanism is specific to React re-parenting and Electron's webview element. In the Go UI the equivalent rule is that htmx swaps never replace the container of a retained widget, and the embedded browser depends on what the system webview offers.

title: Plugin entry customization: region-owned pins and More menus
summary: The left sidebar, the conversation header and the right sidebar guide each keep their own list of hidden plugin entries and draw their own 'More' menu. One plugin supplies the shared menu content, including 'browse plugins' and 'create your plugin'.
firstReason: The feature (hide rarely used entries, per region, persisted) stands. In the Go UI each region is a template that filters its entries from a stored preference; the slot registration that shares the menu content is React-specific.

title: New Session reuses a blank Session, matching a requested preset
summary: New Session reuses the workspace's first blank session, keeping its unsent draft. A request that names a preset skips a blank session that lists a different preset.
firstReason: Creating a fresh session on every click lost the draft, and letting a preset flow take over any blank session moved an ordinary draft under the wrong preset. Inference: with no client store the selection moves into the host, next to the writer-lock rule of the blank-reuse note.

title: The workspace tree is per-pane state drawn inside each file tab, and the plugin mounting it decides where files open
summary: The workspace file tree is drawn inside each file tab, but its state (expansion, width, scroll, last revealed file) is kept per pane, so it survives tab switches. Hidden trees hold no directory watch on the host.
firstReason: State per pane exists because the dock unmounts unselected tabs. The goals (tree state survives tab switches, no watch for a hidden tree) stand; where the state lives in a server-rendered UI is the UI area's decision.

title: Right Sidebar docking infrastructure
summary: The right column of the Web client is a per-session docking surface with split panes, tabs, floating panels and an undoable sequence of layout operations, into which plugins register tab types. It replaced a single-purpose detail panel.
firstReason: A shared side surface where features open tabs (preview, files, terminal, browser) stays a requirement. A drag-and-drop docking engine is client-side JavaScript; the UI area must decide between a small island for the layout and a simpler server-driven model of tabs and splits.

title: Browser Excel preview with saved formula results
summary: Spreadsheets (XLSX, XLS, CSV, TSV) are previewed read-only in the browser with a JavaScript grid and parser libraries, showing each formula with its saved result. The host only serves bounded bytes, and a chart the viewer cannot draw must not block the cells.
firstReason: The preview requirements stand (saved formula results, literal CSV strings, tolerance of unsupported drawings). Upstream parses in the browser to avoid the Office engine; the Go UI must choose between parsing on the host and rendering a table, or keeping a JavaScript island for the grid.

title: Sandboxed Sidebar browser
summary: A `browser` sidebar tab shows a Web page in a sandboxed iframe. The address parser accepts only `http` and `https`, rejects embedded credentials, the application's own origin, `file:` and every other scheme, and chat links open in such a tab when the tab type is registered.
firstReason: An iframe with a sandbox attribute is plain HTML, so the feature and its trust rules carry straight into a server-rendered page. The address rules are a security boundary and should be checked on the host.

title: Host-memory Session reading state
summary: The host keeps one reading record per session in memory and streams it to every client, so unread-completion and failure marks agree across browsers, including for turns that end while no client is connected. Reading activity never enters the session log or the model's history.
firstReason: The state already lives on the host, which is where a server-rendered UI wants it. The area should decide whether in-memory is still enough, because the records are lost when the host restarts.

title: Session panel in the Chat View's end gutter
summary: Facts about the current session (project directory, change requests, outputs) are shown in one floating panel beside the transcript. The panel docks only while the gutter next to the transcript is wide enough; without room, the header button opens it as a temporary overlay.
firstReason: The goal, one home for session facts that does not take width from the transcript, stands. Upstream reaches it with React slots and a gutter width published by the Chat View; the Go host renders the panel as an HTML fragment. A small script is still needed, because the note itself records that docked and overlay differ in behaviour (focus, Escape, outside press) and not only in size.

title: The sidebar scrollbar's delay and fade live in a CSS transition
summary: The sidebar scrollbar thumb stays visible for 500 ms after the pointer leaves and then fades over 200 ms. The delay and fade are a CSS transition on a registered custom property, not a JavaScript timer, and reduced-motion users get the hold followed by an instant switch.
firstReason: Expressing timing in CSS is exactly what a server-rendered UI with little JavaScript wants, and the technique does not depend on React. The Go sidebar can carry the same style rules.
